title: Unit conversion and repeated-event rates
transcript: A rate pairs an amount with a unit of time, distance or work. Convert the units before you multiply, divide or compare. For repeating events, decide whether the start counts and whether the last instant is included.

AMC practice often mixes clocks, seconds, minutes and distances. Read the units printed beside each number before writing an equation. A Mawa style investigation can combine two repeat schedules. Track the shared events as well as the individual schedules.
A trail is two kilometres and three hundred and fifty metres long. What is its length in metres? First convert the kilometres, then add the remaining metres.
Each kilometre has one thousand metres. The kilometre part is two thousand metres. Adding the extra three hundred and fifty metres gives two thousand three hundred and fifty metres in all.

A sensor flashes every thirty-five seconds, with its first flash after one complete interval. Count the flashes in seven minutes, including the finish if there is a flash there. Convert the time window to seconds before dividing.

The window is four hundred and twenty seconds. Each completed interval contains exactly one flash at its end. Divide by thirty-five. There are twelve whole intervals and zero seconds remaining. The count is twelve. At the start the light has not yet flashed, so no extra event belongs at zero.

Two signals flash at time zero. One repeats every seventy seconds, and the other every one hundred and five seconds. In the first fourteen minutes, including both endpoints, how many distinct instants have a flash? Count simultaneous flashes as one instant.

The window is eight hundred and forty seconds. In the first schedule there are twelve later flashes, plus the one at zero. The second schedule gives nine flashes including zero. Both schedules are aligned initially, so they coincide every two hundred and ten seconds. The shared count is five, including the start. Subtract that from the two individual counts to keep one copy of each shared instant.

The overlap uses the least common multiple of seventy seconds and one hundred and five seconds. Both timers complete whole intervals at those instants. The answer is seventeen. A flash at either endpoint is counted once if it is in both schedules.

A minute is sixty seconds, not a hundred. Multiply all time quantities into one shared unit before comparing repeat intervals. A count of full intervals does not include an event at time zero. Add that event if the wording says it belongs.

Write the units next to the numbers. Convert to a common unit and use a short timeline to mark the first repeat. For two schedules, check the shared starts and the repeated overlap. Verify whether the endpoint itself is a legal event.
